::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

- match the type of outcome (continuous, binary, count, time to event) to a regression model;
- explain why logistic regression, not linear regression, is used for a binary outcome;
- interpret odds ratios from simple and adjusted logistic models;
- describe how adjustment addresses confounding and how dummy variables code a categorical predictor;
- test an interaction (effect modification) between two predictors;
- check multicollinearity and influence, and compare nested models with AIC, BIC, and likelihood ratio tests.
:::

## Introduction

Statistical modeling is a fundamental tool in epidemiology that allows us to:

- **Describe** relationships between variables
- **Predict** outcomes based on risk factors
- **Estimate associations** while controlling for confounding

This lecture introduces key concepts in regression modeling using real-world data from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) 2023.

## Setup and Data Preparation

```{r}
#| label: load-packages
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# Load required packages
library(tidyverse)
library(brfssdata)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(plotly)
library(broom)
library(car)
library(ggeffects)
library(ggstats)
```

### Loading BRFSS 2023 Data

The BRFSS is a large-scale telephone survey that collects data on health-related risk behaviors, chronic health conditions, and use of preventive services from U.S. residents.

::: {.data-card}
[Data for this lecture]{.eyebrow}

**BRFSS 2023, loaded with the brfssdata R package.** The first time you run the code below, `read_brfss()` downloads the 2023 survey once and keeps it on your computer. We recode the variables on the full file, keep people with complete data, and draw a random sample of 2,000 adults.

Install the packages once with `install.packages(c("brfssdata", "janitor"))`.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
BRFSS 2023 codebook: [CDC annual data page](https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/annual_data/annual_2023.html). Package documentation: [brfssdata](https://muntasirmasum.github.io/brfssdata/).
:::

Two coding details matter. First, BRFSS uses 7 for "don't know" and 9 for "refused" or "missing", so those codes become `NA` instead of being counted as "no". Second, the question about current smoking (`SMOKDAY2`) is asked only of people who have smoked at least 100 cigarettes (`SMOKE100`); people who never reached 100 cigarettes are coded as not current smokers rather than dropped.

```{r}
#| label: load-data
# Read the BRFSS 2023 variables this lecture uses (CDC names)
brfss_raw <- read_brfss(
  2023,
  vars = c("DIABETE4", "_AGE_G", "_SEX", "_RACE", "_EDUCAG", "_INCOMG1",
           "_BMI5CAT", "EXERANY2", "SMOKE100", "SMOKDAY2", "GENHLTH",
           "_RFHYPE6", "_RFCHOL3")
) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

# Recode on the full file. Codes 7 ("don't know") and 9 ("refused" or
# "missing") become NA so they are never counted as "no".
brfss_recoded <- brfss_raw |>
  mutate(
    # Outcome: diagnosed diabetes (gestational-only and prediabetes count as no)
    diabetes = case_when(
      diabete4 == 1 ~ 1,
      diabete4 %in% c(2, 3, 4) ~ 0
    ),
    age_group = factor(case_when(
      age_g == 1 ~ "18-24",
      age_g == 2 ~ "25-34",
      age_g == 3 ~ "35-44",
      age_g == 4 ~ "45-54",
      age_g == 5 ~ "55-64",
      age_g == 6 ~ "65+"
    ), levels = c("18-24", "25-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55-64", "65+")),
    # Age as a number: the midpoint of each age group
    age_cont = case_when(
      age_g == 1 ~ 21,
      age_g == 2 ~ 29.5,
      age_g == 3 ~ 39.5,
      age_g == 4 ~ 49.5,
      age_g == 5 ~ 59.5,
      age_g == 6 ~ 70
    ),
    sex = factor(ifelse(sex == 1, "Male", "Female")),
    race = factor(case_when(
      race == 1 ~ "White",
      race == 2 ~ "Black",
      race == 3 ~ "Native American",
      race == 4 ~ "Asian",
      race == 5 ~ "Native Hawaiian/PI",
      race == 6 ~ "Other",
      race == 7 ~ "Multiracial",
      race == 8 ~ "Hispanic"
    ), levels = c("White", "Black", "Hispanic", "Asian", "Native American",
                  "Native Hawaiian/PI", "Other", "Multiracial")),
    education = factor(case_when(
      educag == 1 ~ "< High school",
      educag == 2 ~ "High school graduate",
      educag == 3 ~ "Some college",
      educag == 4 ~ "College graduate"
    ), levels = c("< High school", "High school graduate", "Some college", "College graduate")),
    # Income: the seven 2023 categories (9 = don't know or missing)
    income = factor(case_when(
      incomg1 == 1 ~ "< $15,000",
      incomg1 == 2 ~ "$15,000-$24,999",
      incomg1 == 3 ~ "$25,000-$34,999",
      incomg1 == 4 ~ "$35,000-$49,999",
      incomg1 == 5 ~ "$50,000-$99,999",
      incomg1 == 6 ~ "$100,000-$199,999",
      incomg1 == 7 ~ "$200,000+"
    ), levels = c("< $15,000", "$15,000-$24,999", "$25,000-$34,999",
                  "$35,000-$49,999", "$50,000-$99,999", "$100,000-$199,999",
                  "$200,000+")),
    bmi_cat = factor(case_when(
      bmi5cat == 1 ~ "Underweight",
      bmi5cat == 2 ~ "Normal",
      bmi5cat == 3 ~ "Overweight",
      bmi5cat == 4 ~ "Obese"
    ), levels = c("Normal", "Underweight", "Overweight", "Obese")),  # Normal weight is the reference
    # Any physical activity in the past 30 days
    phys_active = case_when(exerany2 == 1 ~ 1, exerany2 == 2 ~ 0),
    # Current smoking: SMOKDAY2 is asked only of people who have smoked at
    # least 100 cigarettes (SMOKE100 = 1), so never-smokers count as 0
    current_smoker = case_when(
      smoke100 == 2 ~ 0,
      smokday2 %in% c(1, 2) ~ 1,
      smokday2 == 3 ~ 0
    ),
    gen_health = factor(case_when(
      genhlth %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Excellent/Very good",
      genhlth == 3 ~ "Good",
      genhlth %in% c(4, 5) ~ "Fair/Poor"
    ), levels = c("Excellent/Very good", "Good", "Fair/Poor")),
    hypertension = case_when(rfhype6 == 2 ~ 1, rfhype6 == 1 ~ 0),
    high_chol = case_when(rfchol3 == 2 ~ 1, rfchol3 == 1 ~ 0)
  )

# Keep complete cases on the analysis variables, then draw 2,000 people
set.seed(553)
brfss_clean <- brfss_recoded |>
  select(diabetes, age_group, age_cont, sex, race, education, income,
         bmi_cat, phys_active, current_smoker, gen_health,
         hypertension, high_chol) |>
  drop_na() |>
  slice_sample(n = 2000)

cat("BRFSS 2023 respondents:", format(nrow(brfss_raw), big.mark = ","), "\n")
cat("Complete cases on the analysis variables:",
    format(nrow(drop_na(select(brfss_recoded, diabetes, age_group, age_cont,
      sex, race, education, income, bmi_cat, phys_active, current_smoker,
      gen_health, hypertension, high_chol))), big.mark = ","), "\n")
cat("Analytic sample:", nrow(brfss_clean), "adults\n")
```

Requiring complete data on all 13 variables also drops people for variables the models below never use, such as income (`r round(100 * mean(is.na(brfss_recoded$income)))`% of respondents did not report it) and cholesterol (`r round(100 * mean(is.na(brfss_recoded$high_chol)))`% missing). A complete-case filter on only the variables each model uses would keep more people.


### Descriptive Statistics

```{r}
#| label: descriptive-stats
# Summary table by diabetes status
desc_table <- brfss_clean |>
  group_by(diabetes) |>
  summarise(
    N = n(),
    `Mean Age` = round(mean(age_cont), 1),
    `% Male` = round(100 * mean(sex == "Male"), 1),
    `% Obese` = round(100 * mean(bmi_cat == "Obese", na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    `% Physically Active` = round(100 * mean(phys_active), 1),
    `% Current Smoker` = round(100 * mean(current_smoker), 1),
    `% Hypertension` = round(100 * mean(hypertension), 1),
    `% High Cholesterol` = round(100 * mean(high_chol), 1)
  ) |>
  mutate(diabetes = ifelse(diabetes == 1, "Diabetes", "No Diabetes"))

desc_table |>
  kable(caption = "Descriptive Statistics by Diabetes Status",
        align = "lrrrrrrrr") |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE)
```

## Part 1: Statistical Modeling Concepts

### 1. What is Statistical Modeling?

A **statistical model** is a mathematical representation of the relationship between:

- An **outcome variable** (dependent variable, response)
- One or more **predictor variables** (independent variables, exposures, covariates)

#### General Form of a Statistical Model

$$f(Y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p + \epsilon$$

Where:

- $f(Y)$ is a function of the outcome (identity, log, logit, etc.)
- $\beta_0$ is the **intercept** (baseline value)
- $\beta_1, \beta_2, \ldots, \beta_p$ are **coefficients** (effect sizes)
- $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_p$ are **predictor variables**
- $\epsilon$ is the **error term** (random variation)

### 2. Types of Regression Models

The choice of regression model depends on the **type of outcome variable**:

```{r}
#| label: model-types-table
#| echo: false
model_types <- data.frame(
  `Outcome Type` = c("Continuous", "Binary", "Count", "Time-to-event"),
  `Regression Type` = c("Linear", "Logistic", "Poisson/Negative Binomial", "Cox Proportional Hazards"),
  `Link Function` = c("Identity: Y", "Logit: log(p/(1-p))", "Log: log(Y)", "Log: log(h(t))"),
  `Example` = c("Blood pressure, BMI", "Disease status, mortality", "Number of infections", "Survival time"),
  check.names = FALSE
)

model_types |>
  kable(caption = "Common Regression Models in Epidemiology",
        align = "llll") |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                full_width = TRUE) |>
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, background = "#f0f0f0", color = "#1f2d3a")
```

#### Simple vs. Multiple Regression

- **Simple regression**: One predictor variable
- **Multiple regression**: Two or more predictor variables (controls for confounding)

### 3. Linear Regression Example

Let's model the relationship between **age** and **diabetes prevalence**.

#### Simple Linear Regression

```{r}
#| label: simple-linear
# Simple linear regression: diabetes ~ age
model_linear_simple <- lm(diabetes ~ age_cont, data = brfss_clean)

# Display results
tidy(model_linear_simple, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  kable(caption = "Simple Linear Regression: Diabetes ~ Age",
        digits = 4,
        col.names = c("Term", "Estimate", "Std. Error", "t-statistic", "p-value", "95% CI Lower", "95% CI Upper")) |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                full_width = FALSE)
```

**Interpretation:**

- **Intercept ($\beta_0$)**: `r round(coef(model_linear_simple)[1], 4)` - Expected probability of diabetes at age 0 (not meaningful in this context)
- **Slope ($\beta_1$)**: `r round(coef(model_linear_simple)[2], 4)` - For each 1-year increase in age, the probability of diabetes `r ifelse(coef(model_linear_simple)[2] > 0, "increases", "decreases")` by `r round(abs(coef(model_linear_simple)[2]) * 100, 2)` percentage points (a linear model for a 0/1 outcome is called a **linear probability model**)

#### Visualization

##### With continuous age

```{r}
#| label: plot-linear-simple
# Create scatter plot with regression line
p1 <- ggplot(brfss_clean, aes(x = age_cont, y = diabetes)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.2, width = 0.5, height = 0.02, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "red", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Age and Diabetes",
    subtitle = "Simple Linear Regression",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Probability of Diabetes"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplotly(p1) |>
  layout(hovermode = "closest")
```

[Figure description: interactive scatter of diabetes (0 or 1, jittered) against age for `r nrow(brfss_clean)` adults, with points in two horizontal bands at 0 and 1 and in six vertical columns at the age-group midpoints. A red linear fit rises from about `r round(100 * predict(model_linear_simple, data.frame(age_cont = 21)))`% at age 21 to about `r round(100 * predict(model_linear_simple, data.frame(age_cont = 70)))`% at age 70.]{.visually-hidden}

### 4. Logistic Regression: The Preferred Model for Binary Outcomes

**Problem with linear regression for binary outcomes:**

- Predicted probabilities can fall outside [0, 1]
- Assumes constant variance (violated for binary data)

**Solution: Logistic Regression**

Uses the **logit link function** to ensure predicted probabilities stay between 0 and 1:

$$\text{logit}(p) = \log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p$$

#### Simple Logistic Regression

```{r}
#| label: simple-logistic
# Simple logistic regression: diabetes ~ age
model_logistic_simple <- glm(diabetes ~ age_cont,
                              data = brfss_clean,
                              family = binomial(link = "logit"))

# Display results with odds ratios
tidy(model_logistic_simple, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  kable(caption = "Simple Logistic Regression: Diabetes ~ Age (Odds Ratios)",
        digits = 3,
        col.names = c("Term", "Odds Ratio", "Std. Error", "z-statistic", "p-value", "95% CI Lower", "95% CI Upper")) |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                full_width = FALSE)
```

**Interpretation:**

- **Odds Ratio (OR)**: `r round(exp(coef(model_logistic_simple)[2]), 3)`
- For each 1-year increase in age, the **odds of diabetes** `r ifelse(coef(model_logistic_simple)[2] > 0, "increase", "decrease")` by `r round(abs(exp(coef(model_logistic_simple)[2]) - 1) * 100, 1)`%
- The association is `r ifelse(tidy(model_logistic_simple)$p.value[2] < 0.05, "statistically significant", "not statistically significant")` (`r ifelse(tidy(model_logistic_simple)$p.value[2] < 0.001, "p < 0.001", paste("p =", signif(tidy(model_logistic_simple)$p.value[2], 2)))`)

#### Predicted Probabilities

```{r}
#| label: fig-pp-age
#| fig-cap: "Predicted probability of diabetes by age (ggeffects)"
#| fig-alt: !expr sprintf("Line with a shaded 95%% confidence band showing the predicted probability of diabetes from the simple logistic model, rising from about %d%% at age 21 to about %d%% at age 70, with the band widening steadily from age 21 to age 70.", round(100 * predict(model_logistic_simple, data.frame(age_cont = 21), type = "response")), round(100 * predict(model_logistic_simple, data.frame(age_cont = 70), type = "response")))
# From ggeffects package
pp <- predict_response(model_logistic_simple, terms = "age_cont")
plot(pp)
```

The same curve can be built by hand with `predict()`. The 95% confidence band is computed on the log-odds scale and then transformed, so it always stays between 0 and 1.

```{r}
#| label: pred-by-hand
# Predicted probabilities with a 95% confidence band
pred_data <- data.frame(age_cont = seq(18, 80, by = 1))
pred_link <- predict(model_logistic_simple, newdata = pred_data,
                     type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
pred_data <- pred_data |>
  mutate(
    predicted_prob = plogis(pred_link$fit),
    lower = plogis(pred_link$fit - 1.96 * pred_link$se.fit),
    upper = plogis(pred_link$fit + 1.96 * pred_link$se.fit)
  )

# Plot
p2 <- ggplot(pred_data, aes(x = age_cont, y = predicted_prob)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
              alpha = 0.2, fill = "darkred") +
  geom_line(color = "darkred", linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Probability of Diabetes by Age",
    subtitle = "Simple logistic regression with 95% confidence band",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Predicted Probability of Diabetes"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplotly(p2)
```

[Figure description: interactive version of the same curve, built with predict(). The predicted probability of diabetes rises from `r round(100 * pred_data$predicted_prob[pred_data$age_cont == 18])`% at age 18 to `r round(100 * pred_data$predicted_prob[pred_data$age_cont == 80])`% at age 80, with a shaded 95% confidence band around the line.]{.visually-hidden}

### 5. Multiple Regression: Controlling for Confounding

#### What is Confounding?

A **confounder** is a variable that:

1. Is associated with both the exposure and the outcome
2. Is not on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome
3. Distorts the true relationship between exposure and outcome

**Example:** The relationship between age and diabetes may be confounded by BMI, physical activity, and other factors.

#### Multiple Logistic Regression

```{r}
#| label: multiple-logistic
# Multiple logistic regression with potential confounders
model_logistic_multiple <- glm(diabetes ~ age_cont + sex + bmi_cat +
                                phys_active + current_smoker + education,
                               data = brfss_clean,
                               family = binomial(link = "logit"))

# Display results
tidy(model_logistic_multiple, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  kable(caption = "Multiple Logistic Regression: Diabetes ~ Age + Covariates (Odds Ratios)",
        digits = 3,
        col.names = c("Term", "Odds Ratio", "Std. Error", "z-statistic", "p-value", "95% CI Lower", "95% CI Upper")) |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                full_width = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: multi-values
#| echo: false
or_obese <- exp(coef(model_logistic_multiple)["bmi_catObese"])
or_age_adj <- exp(coef(model_logistic_multiple)["age_cont"])
or_male <- exp(coef(model_logistic_multiple)["sexMale"])
p_multi <- summary(model_logistic_multiple)$coefficients[, "Pr(>|z|)"]
fmt_p <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "p < 0.001" else paste0("p = ", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))
```

**Interpretation:**

- **Age (adjusted OR)**: `r round(or_age_adj, 3)`
  - After adjusting for sex, BMI, physical activity, smoking, and education, each 1-year increase in age is associated with a `r round(abs(or_age_adj - 1) * 100, 1)`% `r ifelse(or_age_adj > 1, "increase", "decrease")` in the odds of diabetes (`r fmt_p(p_multi["age_cont"])`)

- **Sex (Male vs Female)**: OR = `r round(or_male, 3)`
  - Males have `r round(abs(or_male - 1) * 100, 1)`% `r ifelse(or_male > 1, "higher", "lower")` odds of diabetes than females, adjusting for the other variables (`r fmt_p(p_multi["sexMale"])`)

- **BMI (Obese vs Normal)**: OR = `r round(or_obese, 3)`
  - Obese individuals had `r round(or_obese, 2)` times the odds of diabetes of normal-weight individuals (`r fmt_p(p_multi["bmi_catObese"])`).

### 6. Dummy Variables: Coding Categorical Predictors

Categorical variables with $k$ levels are represented using $k-1$ **dummy variables** (indicator variables).

#### Example: Education Level

Education has 4 levels:

1. < High school (reference category)
2. High school graduate
3. Some college
4. College graduate

R automatically creates 3 dummy variables:

```{r}
#| label: dummy-variables
# Extract dummy variable coding
dummy_table <- data.frame(
  Education = c("< High school", "High school graduate", "Some college", "College graduate"),
  `Dummy 1 (HS grad)` = c(0, 1, 0, 0),
  `Dummy 2 (Some college)` = c(0, 0, 1, 0),
  `Dummy 3 (College grad)` = c(0, 0, 0, 1),
  check.names = FALSE
)

dummy_table |>
  kable(caption = "Dummy Variable Coding for Education",
        align = "lccc") |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                full_width = FALSE) |>
  row_spec(1, bold = TRUE, background = "#ffe6e6", color = "#1f2d3a")  # Highlight reference category
```

**Reference Category:** The category with all zeros (< High school) is the **reference group**. All other categories are compared to this reference.

#### Visualizing Education Effects

```{r}
#| label: plot-education-effects
# Extract education coefficients
educ_coefs <- tidy(model_logistic_multiple, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(str_detect(term, "education")) |>
  mutate(
    education_level = str_remove(term, "education"),
    education_level = factor(education_level,
                             levels = c("High school graduate",
                                       "Some college",
                                       "College graduate"))
  )

# Add reference category
ref_row <- data.frame(
  term = "education< High school",
  estimate = 1.0,
  std.error = 0,
  statistic = NA,
  p.value = NA,
  conf.low = 1.0,
  conf.high = 1.0,
  education_level = factor("< High school (Ref)",
                          levels = c("< High school (Ref)",
                                    "High school graduate",
                                    "Some college",
                                    "College graduate"))
)

educ_coefs_full <- bind_rows(ref_row, educ_coefs) |>
  mutate(education_level = factor(education_level,
                                 levels = c("< High school (Ref)",
                                           "High school graduate",
                                           "Some college",
                                           "College graduate")))

# Plot
p3 <- ggplot(educ_coefs_full, aes(x = education_level, y = estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
                  size = 0.8, color = "darkblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Association Between Education and Diabetes",
    subtitle = "Adjusted Odds Ratios (reference: < High school)",
    x = "Education Level",
    y = "Odds Ratio (95% CI)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplotly(p3)
```

[Figure description: interactive dot-and-interval plot of adjusted odds ratios for diabetes by education, with less than high school as the reference (odds ratio 1, dashed line). High school graduate `r sprintf("%.2f", educ_coefs$estimate[1])` (95% CI `r sprintf("%.2f", educ_coefs$conf.low[1])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", educ_coefs$conf.high[1])`), some college `r sprintf("%.2f", educ_coefs$estimate[2])` (`r sprintf("%.2f", educ_coefs$conf.low[2])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", educ_coefs$conf.high[2])`), college graduate `r sprintf("%.2f", educ_coefs$estimate[3])` (`r sprintf("%.2f", educ_coefs$conf.low[3])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", educ_coefs$conf.high[3])`).]{.visually-hidden}

```{r}
#| label: fig-ggcoef
#| fig-cap: "Education odds ratios drawn with ggcoef_model()"
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-alt: !expr sprintf("Forest plot from ggcoef_model of the adjusted odds ratios for education, on a log scale with a vertical line at 1. Less than high school is the reference. High school graduate %.2f, some college %.2f, and college graduate %.2f, each with a 95%% confidence interval.", educ_coefs$estimate[1], educ_coefs$estimate[2], educ_coefs$estimate[3])
# Plot model coefficients with `ggcoef_model()`
ggcoef_model(model_logistic_multiple, exponentiate = TRUE,
  include = c("education"),
  variable_labels = c(
    education = "Education"),
  facet_labeller = ggplot2::label_wrap_gen(10)
)
```

### 7. Interactions (Effect Modification)

An **interaction** exists when the effect of one variable on the outcome differs across levels of another variable.

**Epidemiologic term:** Effect modification

#### Example: Age × Sex Interaction

Does the effect of age on diabetes differ between males and females?

```{r}
#| label: interaction-model
# Model with interaction term
model_interaction <- glm(diabetes ~ age_cont * sex + bmi_cat + phys_active,
                         data = brfss_clean,
                         family = binomial(link = "logit"))

# Display interaction results
tidy(model_interaction, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(str_detect(term, "age_cont")) |>
  kable(caption = "Age × Sex Interaction Model (Odds Ratios)",
        digits = 3,
        col.names = c("Term", "Odds Ratio", "Std. Error", "z-statistic", "p-value", "95% CI Lower", "95% CI Upper")) |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                full_width = FALSE)
```

**Interpretation:**

- **Main effect of age**: OR among females (reference)
- **Interaction term (age:sexMale)**: Additional effect of age among males
- If the interaction term is significant, the age-diabetes relationship differs by sex

**In these data:** the interaction odds ratio is `r round(exp(coef(model_interaction)["age_cont:sexMale"]), 3)` (`r fmt_p(summary(model_interaction)$coefficients["age_cont:sexMale", "Pr(>|z|)"])`), so `r ifelse(summary(model_interaction)$coefficients["age_cont:sexMale", "Pr(>|z|)"] < 0.05, "the age-diabetes association differs significantly between males and females", "there is no statistically significant evidence that the age-diabetes association differs between males and females")`.

#### Visualizing Interaction

```{r}
#| label: plot-interaction
# Generate predicted probabilities by sex
pred_interact <- ggpredict(model_interaction, terms = c("age_cont [18:80]", "sex"))

# Plot
p4 <- ggplot(pred_interact, aes(x = x, y = predicted, color = group, fill = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2, color = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Probability of Diabetes by Age and Sex",
    subtitle = "Testing for Age × Sex Interaction",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Predicted Probability of Diabetes",
    color = "Sex",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Female" = "#E64B35", "Male" = "#4DBBD5")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Female" = "#E64B35", "Male" = "#4DBBD5")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

ggplotly(p4)
```

[Figure description: interactive line chart of predicted probability of diabetes by age, one line per sex with shaded 95% confidence bands. Females rise from `r round(100 * pred_interact$predicted[pred_interact$x == 18 & pred_interact$group == "Female"])`% at age 18 to `r round(100 * pred_interact$predicted[pred_interact$x == 80 & pred_interact$group == "Female"])`% at age 80; males from `r round(100 * pred_interact$predicted[pred_interact$x == 18 & pred_interact$group == "Male"])`% to `r round(100 * pred_interact$predicted[pred_interact$x == 80 & pred_interact$group == "Male"])`%. The bands overlap across most of the age range.]{.visually-hidden}

### 8. Model Diagnostics

Every regression model makes **assumptions about the data**. If assumptions are violated, results may be invalid.

#### Key Assumptions for Logistic Regression

1. **Linearity of log odds**: Continuous predictors have a linear relationship with the log odds of the outcome
2. **Independence of observations**: Each observation is independent
3. **No perfect multicollinearity**: Predictors are not perfectly correlated
4. **No influential outliers**: Individual observations don't overly influence the model

#### Checking for Multicollinearity

**Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)**: Measures how much the variance of a coefficient is inflated due to correlation with other predictors.

- **VIF < 5**: Generally acceptable
- **VIF > 10**: Serious multicollinearity problem

```{r}
#| label: vif-check
# Calculate VIF
vif_values <- vif(model_logistic_multiple)

# Create VIF table
# For models with categorical variables, vif() returns GVIF (Generalized VIF)
if (is.matrix(vif_values)) {
  # If matrix (categorical variables present), extract GVIF^(1/(2*Df))
  vif_df <- data.frame(
    Variable = rownames(vif_values),
    VIF = vif_values[, "GVIF^(1/(2*Df))"],
    row.names = NULL
  )
} else {
  # If vector (only continuous variables)
  vif_df <- data.frame(
    Variable = names(vif_values),
    VIF = as.numeric(vif_values)
  )
}

# Add interpretation
vif_df <- vif_df |>
  arrange(desc(VIF)) |>
  mutate(
    Interpretation = case_when(
      VIF < 5 ~ "Low (No concern)",
      VIF >= 5 & VIF < 10 ~ "Moderate (Monitor)",
      VIF >= 10 ~ "High (Problem)"
    )
  )

vif_df |>
  kable(caption = "Variance Inflation Factors (VIF) for Multiple Regression Model",
        digits = 2,
        align = "lrc") |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                full_width = FALSE) |>
  row_spec(which(vif_df$VIF >= 10), bold = TRUE, color = "white", background = "#B0213C") |>
  row_spec(which(vif_df$VIF >= 5 & vif_df$VIF < 10), background = "#FFD8A8", color = "#1f2d3a") |>
  row_spec(which(vif_df$VIF < 5), background = "#D4EDDA", color = "#1f2d3a")
```

#### Influential Observations

**Cook's Distance**: Measures how much the model would change if an observation were removed.

- **Cook's D > 1**: Potentially influential observation

```{r}
#| label: cooks-distance
# Calculate Cook's distance
cooks_d <- cooks.distance(model_logistic_multiple)

# Create data frame
influence_df <- data.frame(
  observation = 1:length(cooks_d),
  cooks_d = cooks_d
) |>
  mutate(influential = ifelse(cooks_d > 1, "Yes", "No"))

# Plot
p5 <- ggplot(influence_df, aes(x = observation, y = cooks_d, color = influential)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Cook's Distance: Identifying Influential Observations",
    subtitle = "Values > 1 indicate potentially influential observations",
    x = "Observation Number",
    y = "Cook's Distance",
    color = "Influential?"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("No" = "steelblue", "Yes" = "red")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplotly(p5)

# Count influential observations
n_influential <- sum(influence_df$influential == "Yes")
cat("Number of potentially influential observations:", n_influential, "\n")
```

[Figure description: interactive scatter of Cook's distance for each of the `r nrow(influence_df)` observations, with a dashed red line at 1. The largest value is `r signif(max(influence_df$cooks_d), 2)`, far below the line, so `r n_influential` observations are flagged as influential.]{.visually-hidden}

### 9. Model Comparison and Selection

#### Comparing Nested Models

Use **Likelihood Ratio Test** to compare nested models:

```{r}
#| label: model-comparison
# Model 1: Age only
model1 <- glm(diabetes ~ age_cont,
              data = brfss_clean,
              family = binomial)

# Model 2: Age + Sex
model2 <- glm(diabetes ~ age_cont + sex,
              data = brfss_clean,
              family = binomial)

# Model 3: Full model
model3 <- model_logistic_multiple

# Likelihood ratio test
lrt_1_2 <- anova(model1, model2, test = "LRT")
lrt_2_3 <- anova(model2, model3, test = "LRT")

# Create comparison table
model_comp <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Model 1: Age only",
            "Model 2: Age + Sex",
            "Model 3: Full model"),
  AIC = c(AIC(model1), AIC(model2), AIC(model3)),
  BIC = c(BIC(model1), BIC(model2), BIC(model3)),
  `Deviance` = c(deviance(model1), deviance(model2), deviance(model3)),
  check.names = FALSE
)

model_comp |>
  kable(caption = "Model Comparison: AIC, BIC, and Deviance",
        digits = 2,
        align = "lrrr") |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                full_width = FALSE) |>
  row_spec(which.min(model_comp$AIC), bold = TRUE, background = "#d4edda", color = "#1f2d3a")
```

**Interpretation:**

- **Lower AIC/BIC** indicates better model fit
- `r if (which.min(model_comp$AIC) == which.min(model_comp$BIC)) paste0(model_comp$Model[which.min(model_comp$AIC)], " has both the lowest AIC (", round(min(model_comp$AIC), 1), ") and the lowest BIC (", round(min(model_comp$BIC), 1), ")") else paste0(model_comp$Model[which.min(model_comp$AIC)], " has the lowest AIC (", round(min(model_comp$AIC), 1), "), but ", model_comp$Model[which.min(model_comp$BIC)], " has the lowest BIC (", round(min(model_comp$BIC), 1), "); BIC penalizes extra terms more")`
- The likelihood ratio test of Model 3 against Model 2 gives `r fmt_p(lrt_2_3$"Pr(>Chi)"[2])`: `r ifelse(lrt_2_3$"Pr(>Chi)"[2] < 0.05, "the added covariates significantly improve the fit", "the added covariates do not significantly improve the fit")`

### 10. Error Term in Statistical Models

All statistical models include an **error term** ($\epsilon$) to account for:

- **Random variation** in the outcome
- **Unmeasured variables** not included in the model
- **Measurement error** in variables

$$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p + \epsilon$$

**Key points:**

- The model cannot perfectly predict every outcome
- The difference between **observed** and **predicted** values is the error (residual)
- We assume errors are normally distributed with mean 0 (for linear regression)

## Part 2: Student Lab Activity

### Lab Overview

In this lab, you will:

1. Build your own logistic regression model predicting **hypertension** (high blood pressure)
2. Create dummy variables for categorical predictors
3. Interpret regression coefficients
4. Test for confounding and interaction
5. Perform model diagnostics

### Lab Setup

Put this code at the top of your lab `.qmd`. It builds the same 2,000-person sample as the lecture (install the packages once with `install.packages(c("brfssdata", "janitor"))`).

```{r}
#| label: lab-setup
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
library(brfssdata)
library(broom)
library(car)
library(ggeffects)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

# Read the BRFSS 2023 variables this lecture uses (CDC names)
brfss_raw <- read_brfss(
  2023,
  vars = c("DIABETE4", "_AGE_G", "_SEX", "_RACE", "_EDUCAG", "_INCOMG1",
           "_BMI5CAT", "EXERANY2", "SMOKE100", "SMOKDAY2", "GENHLTH",
           "_RFHYPE6", "_RFCHOL3")
) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

# Recode on the full file. Codes 7 ("don't know") and 9 ("refused" or
# "missing") become NA so they are never counted as "no".
brfss_recoded <- brfss_raw |>
  mutate(
    # Outcome: diagnosed diabetes (gestational-only and prediabetes count as no)
    diabetes = case_when(
      diabete4 == 1 ~ 1,
      diabete4 %in% c(2, 3, 4) ~ 0
    ),
    age_group = factor(case_when(
      age_g == 1 ~ "18-24",
      age_g == 2 ~ "25-34",
      age_g == 3 ~ "35-44",
      age_g == 4 ~ "45-54",
      age_g == 5 ~ "55-64",
      age_g == 6 ~ "65+"
    ), levels = c("18-24", "25-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55-64", "65+")),
    # Age as a number: the midpoint of each age group
    age_cont = case_when(
      age_g == 1 ~ 21,
      age_g == 2 ~ 29.5,
      age_g == 3 ~ 39.5,
      age_g == 4 ~ 49.5,
      age_g == 5 ~ 59.5,
      age_g == 6 ~ 70
    ),
    sex = factor(ifelse(sex == 1, "Male", "Female")),
    race = factor(case_when(
      race == 1 ~ "White",
      race == 2 ~ "Black",
      race == 3 ~ "Native American",
      race == 4 ~ "Asian",
      race == 5 ~ "Native Hawaiian/PI",
      race == 6 ~ "Other",
      race == 7 ~ "Multiracial",
      race == 8 ~ "Hispanic"
    ), levels = c("White", "Black", "Hispanic", "Asian", "Native American",
                  "Native Hawaiian/PI", "Other", "Multiracial")),
    education = factor(case_when(
      educag == 1 ~ "< High school",
      educag == 2 ~ "High school graduate",
      educag == 3 ~ "Some college",
      educag == 4 ~ "College graduate"
    ), levels = c("< High school", "High school graduate", "Some college", "College graduate")),
    # Income: the seven 2023 categories (9 = don't know or missing)
    income = factor(case_when(
      incomg1 == 1 ~ "< $15,000",
      incomg1 == 2 ~ "$15,000-$24,999",
      incomg1 == 3 ~ "$25,000-$34,999",
      incomg1 == 4 ~ "$35,000-$49,999",
      incomg1 == 5 ~ "$50,000-$99,999",
      incomg1 == 6 ~ "$100,000-$199,999",
      incomg1 == 7 ~ "$200,000+"
    ), levels = c("< $15,000", "$15,000-$24,999", "$25,000-$34,999",
                  "$35,000-$49,999", "$50,000-$99,999", "$100,000-$199,999",
                  "$200,000+")),
    bmi_cat = factor(case_when(
      bmi5cat == 1 ~ "Underweight",
      bmi5cat == 2 ~ "Normal",
      bmi5cat == 3 ~ "Overweight",
      bmi5cat == 4 ~ "Obese"
    ), levels = c("Normal", "Underweight", "Overweight", "Obese")),  # Normal weight is the reference
    # Any physical activity in the past 30 days
    phys_active = case_when(exerany2 == 1 ~ 1, exerany2 == 2 ~ 0),
    # Current smoking: SMOKDAY2 is asked only of people who have smoked at
    # least 100 cigarettes (SMOKE100 = 1), so never-smokers count as 0
    current_smoker = case_when(
      smoke100 == 2 ~ 0,
      smokday2 %in% c(1, 2) ~ 1,
      smokday2 == 3 ~ 0
    ),
    gen_health = factor(case_when(
      genhlth %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Excellent/Very good",
      genhlth == 3 ~ "Good",
      genhlth %in% c(4, 5) ~ "Fair/Poor"
    ), levels = c("Excellent/Very good", "Good", "Fair/Poor")),
    hypertension = case_when(rfhype6 == 2 ~ 1, rfhype6 == 1 ~ 0),
    high_chol = case_when(rfchol3 == 2 ~ 1, rfchol3 == 1 ~ 0)
  )

# Keep complete cases on the analysis variables, then draw 2,000 people
set.seed(553)
brfss_clean <- brfss_recoded |>
  select(diabetes, age_group, age_cont, sex, race, education, income,
         bmi_cat, phys_active, current_smoker, gen_health,
         hypertension, high_chol) |>
  drop_na() |>
  slice_sample(n = 2000)
```

## Summary

### Key Concepts Covered

1. **Statistical modeling** describes relationships between variables
2. **Regression types** depend on the outcome variable type
3. **Logistic regression** is appropriate for binary outcomes
4. **Multiple regression** controls for confounding
5. **Dummy variables** represent categorical predictors
6. **Interactions** test for effect modification
7. **Model diagnostics** check assumptions and identify problems
8. **Model comparison** helps select the best model

### Important Formulas

**Logistic Regression:**

$$\text{logit}(p) = \log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p$$

**Odds Ratio:**

$$\text{OR} = e^{\beta_i}$$

**Predicted Probability:**

$$p = \frac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p}}$$

- Vittinghoff, E., Glidden, D. V., Shiboski, S. C., & McCulloch, C. E. (2012). *Regression Methods in Biostatistics* (2nd ed.). Springer.
- Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. (2023). *Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System*.
